name: Cobalt Blue
lede: Cobalt blue is the paint made by firing cobalt with alumina, worked out in Vienna, Freiberg and Paris between 1775 and 1802; the dark navy swatch shown here is a chart's sample of the name, much darker than a tube of the pigment.

sections.title: Two swatches, one name
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is a dark, slightly purplish navy, #232D53 [20]. It comes from the RAL standard, where it is number 5013 and dates from 1927, and from Maerz and Paul's color dictionary of 1930, which records the name from 1777 [20]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 also lists it [20].

That is not the blue most people picture. The cobalt blue in the 2010 xkcd color survey, kept in our library as an alternate, is a vivid, pure blue, #030AA7, about 17 units away [20]. The other cobalt on this site, [[cobalt]], is #0047AB, about 15 units away [20]. And George Field described the real pigment in 1835 as a blue that leans neither toward green nor toward purple and rivals the best ultramarine in brilliance [9]. This swatch is a chart's dark sample of the name, not the paint.

In the library the same swatch also carries a Japanese traditional name, *rurikon*, which means a dark lapis-lazuli blue [20].

sections.title: The names it collected
sections.body:
The metal is named from German *kobold*, a ghost or goblin, and Paterson places that usage in Bohemia [12]. The pigment then collected the names of the people credited with it. In Paterson's list it appears as Dresden blue, King's blue and Thénard's blue [12]. The Compendium adds Leithner's, Gahn's, Wenzel's and Binder's blues, Königsblau, new blue, and Vienna blue, the last for a version made with arsenic [1][2].

Be careful with King's blue, because Paterson also gives that name to a pale blue made of ultramarine and Cremnitz white [12]. Reckitt's blue is a cobalt blue named after Francis Reckitt, and also a trade name for a laundry whitener [12]. Charron blue, a mix of cobalt blue and barium sulphate, was one of the colors Gauguin used [12][4]. In the Colour Index the pigment is number 77346 [1].

sections.title: Four names for one reaction
sections.body:
The Compendium gives the earliest modern history [1]. Leithner in Vienna appears to have found the basic process, calcining cobalt oxide with alumina, in 1775 [1]. Just before 1777 the Swedish chemist Gahn saw that aluminium compounds moistened with a cobalt solution turned blue when strongly heated, and C. F. Wenzel in Freiberg found the same reaction at almost the same time [1]. By Binder's account the manufacturers of Saxony used a similar process and treated it as a secret [1].

Other books start the story in 1802 [3][9]. Ball, St Clair, Coles and Paterson all credit the French chemist Louis-Jacques Thénard, who was set by the minister Chaptal to find a cheaper blue than ultramarine [3][9][11][12][13]. He knew that the potters of Sèvres used cobalt in their blue glazes, and roasting a cobalt arsenate or phosphate with alumina gave him a deep, fine blue [9]. Pastoureau splits the difference, writing that cobalt blue was discovered or rediscovered in 1802 [15]. The Compendium dates Thénard's published method a year later, to 1803, and says it improved on earlier ways by using cobalt phosphate or arsenate in place of carbonate or nitrate [1].

Priority fights did not stop there. In 1911 McEachern claimed that adding magnesium salts improved the color, and Vanino replied that he and Wagner had worked on the same change since 1908 [1]. The Maerz and Paul date of 1777 for the name, a year after Gahn and Wenzel were at work, fits the earlier makers better than Thénard [20][1]. Books disagree, then, not about the chemistry but about whom to credit.

sections.title: What a tube of it contains
sections.body:
Many compounds and processes have been sold under the heading cobalt blue [1]. Today the name means cobalt aluminate, CoO·Al2O3, and close variants of it [1]. Older writers also filed smalt and the cobalt tin oxide now called cerulean blue under the same word, and potters use it for glazes and enamels, which are not pigments in the painter's sense [1]. Paterson lists a cobalt turquoise, which is cobalt titanium oxide [12].

Names on tubes have never been a safe guide. Ball notes that paint makers took to naming new pigments after classical ones, as though cobalt blue were a hue and not a substance, and he quotes Doerner's complaint of 1934 about arbitrary and fantastic names [8]. Gurney's rule is that the word *hue* on a tube warns of a mixture standing in for a costlier pigment [18]. His palettes use the Colour Index code PB 28 for the real pigment [17].

It is among the most durable blues. The Compendium calls it extremely stable and says it strongly promotes the curing of drying oils [1]. Ball says that cobalt blue and lemon yellow aged very well among the new pigments, while zinc yellow turned greenish [6]. It was always dear, though. Ball calls it expensive but popular, and by the 1870s artificial ultramarine, which cost less, was the standard painter's blue [3][5].

Livingstone explains an odd fact of its looks. Cobalt blue reflects well into the green, which should make it look greenish, but it also reflects some red, and red and cyan cancel in the visual system, leaving a pure blue [16].

sections.title: The painters' blue of the nineteenth century
sections.body:
Painters took it up fast. William Blake's early biographer listed it among his few pigments [14], and Turner used it within a few years of its introduction [3]. In the Pre-Raphaelite *Ophelia* of 1851 to 1852, Millais used it among new materials, and Holman Hunt put it in *The Awakening Conscience* of 1853 [3]. Ball counts twelve new synthetic colors among the twenty main pigments found in Impressionist pictures, and cobalt blue is one of them [4].

It suited the Impressionist method of unmixed color [4]. In Renoir's *Boating on the Seine*, of 1879 to 1880, the river is nearly pure cobalt blue with a little white, glazed with red lake for the purple shadows, against the chrome orange of a boat [4]. In Monet's *Lavacourt under Snow* of about 1879 the brightest snow is pure cobalt [4]. Impressionists tended to make their violets by glazing cobalt blue or ultramarine with red lake; Renoir kept that mixture for the purples of *At the Theatre* and *The Umbrellas*, while Monet favored the new cobalt violet more than most [4]. Van Gogh preferred to approximate cerulean with cobalt blue, a little cadmium yellow and white [10]. The Australian painter Arthur Streeton, with no charcoal, drew out a composition in red and cobalt blue [19].

Cobalt blue had a cheaper rival. Once artificial ultramarine appeared in France from 1828 it undercut natural ultramarine by a wide margin, and by the 1870s it was the standard painter's blue, even more than cobalt, which cost appreciably more [5]. Jean-Georges Vibert's 1891 list of pigments that would keep their brilliance included cobalt blue [3].

sections.title: Rubens, Vermeer and the forger
sections.body:
A persistent error puts cobalt blue on the palette of Rubens [7]. Ball points out that Birren's history of painting hands the pigment to Rubens and his generation, roughly two hundred years too early, and he suggests Birren probably meant smalt, a cobalt glass that is a different, inferior blue [7]. The Pigment Compendium's habit of listing both under one heading shows how easily the two get tangled [1].

Cobalt blue also helped convict a forger. In 1945 Han van Meegeren confessed that the Vermeer sold to Göring was his own work, and one giveaway was a blue that was not made until about 130 years after Vermeer's death [9]. Finlay adds a twist: the ultramarine he bought was already adulterated with cobalt, so the paint was both his undoing and, as his lawyer argued, his defense [23].

sections.title: Cerulean and the other cobalts
sections.body: Chemists soon learned that cobalt gives other colors. Cobalt green, with zinc oxide in place of alumina, had been found by the Swedish chemist Sven Rinmann in 1780 but was practical only once zinc oxide was made in quantity, from 1835 [3][11]. Cobalt violet followed in about 1860 [12]. The cobalt tin blue called cerulean was sold as a watercolor by Rowney in the 1860s and as an oil color by the 1870s, as cerulean in England and *bleu céleste* in France [3]. Coles calls its slight green the natural foil for the red in cobalt blue [11]. See [[cerulean-blue]], [[cobalt-green]] and [[manganese-violet]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
On screen this swatch has a lightness of 19.5 on the 100-point scale, with a hue of 289 degrees, firmly between blue and violet [20]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[navy]] at 2.5 units, then Mascot and Deep Navy [20]. Among gems the closest twin is a deep [[gem:azurite|azurite]], 1.4 units away [20].

Our archive cannot see pigments, only photographs of aged, varnished paintings, but its numbers are still suggestive. In 62 of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas [21]. In 79 per cent of those it plays the shadow, the darkest of the painting's main colors [21]. The 1900s carry it at about four times the archive's rate, in 18 of 1,674 paintings, and Impressionism shows it in 2 of 140 [21].

The largest matches are Jawlensky's *[[painting:nga-54131|Murnau]]* of 1910, with the color covering nearly 38 per cent of the canvas, and Netscher's *[[painting:smk-KMSsp670|A Young Turk]]*, painted in 1683, at about 35 per cent [21]. Vilhelm Lundstrøm is the surprise: three of his 17 works in the archive carry it, 68 times the expected rate [21]. The earliest match is Pietro Lorenzetti's *[[painting:commons-Q3842761|Madonna and Child Enthroned with Eight Angels]]* of 1340, 437 years before the earliest date Maerz and Paul give for the name [21][20]. That is the caveat in action: a dark blue of that age is a color, not cobalt.

origin.named_after: the metal cobalt, from German kobold (goblin)
origin.first_recorded: as a pigment, Leithner 1775, Gahn and Wenzel before 1777, Thénard 1802-03 (books disagree); Maerz & Paul record the color name from 1777
origin.source: Pigment Compendium, "Cobalt blue"; Ball, Bright Earth; Maerz & Paul 1930

questions.q: A painting said to be by Rubens contains cobalt blue. What does that tell a conservator?
choices: The blue is a later addition or the picture is not by Rubens: the pigment is almost two centuries younger
Nothing: cobalt blue was in every Baroque studio
It proves the painting is authentic
questions.answer: The blue is a later addition or the picture is not by Rubens: the pigment is almost two centuries younger

questions.q: What does the word hue usually warn of on a tube labeled cobalt blue hue?
choices: A mixture standing in for the real pigment
A transparent version of cobalt blue
questions.answer: A mixture standing in for the real pigment

questions.q: Cobalt blue, unlike zinc yellow, aged very well in nineteenth-century paintings.

openers: A forger was caught partly by a blue that did not exist until about 130 years after Vermeer died: cobalt blue.
Renoir painted the river in Boating on the Seine in almost pure cobalt blue, then glazed it with red lake for the purple shadows.
Three screen colors share the name cobalt blue, from vivid blue to dark navy; the pigment Field described in 1835 leaned neither green nor purple.
